Trump says Iran war will end soon, US military insists Hormuz is secure
Trump says Iran war will end soon, US military insists Hormuz is secure
US president says there will be no military strike against Iran prior to elections
Commander of US military in Middle East says he did not see any Iranian military presence in Strait of Hormuz
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said on Friday that he ‌believed the ‌war with ‌Iran will end soon despite reports that the US and Israel are planning a fresh round or strikes.
“It's going to get wrapped ‌up ‌soon,” Trump ‌said in ‌an interview with a Kansas City radio station as he campaigned ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“We ‌need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon,” he added.
Trump has said the US would not strike Iran before the elections, with the conflict proving a key issue during campaigning.
His comments come amid a wave of diplomacy in the region to try and break the stand-off coupled with reports of a possible new military campaign against Iran once the midterms are finished.
The US military’s senior officer overseeing the Middle East, Adm. Brad Cooper, met Trump at the White House on Thursday to outline military options in Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The US-Iran war has become focussed on shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz where Iran attempted to stop energy exports from the region in response to the initial US-Israeli attacks.
Washington has managed to create a protected shipping route through the strait, which has allowed oil shipments to climb back to their pre-war levels despite ongoing Iranian attacks.
At the same time, the US says it has completely cut off oil exports from Iran with its own blockade.
Cooper, the head of the Pentagon's Central Command, said on Friday that during a recent flight he took over the Strait of Hormuz there was no Iranian military presence because “Iran’s Navy is all at the bottom of the sea.”
“I saw dozens of commercial vessels transiting. All types. Cargo, crude oil, liquid natural gas, or LNG,” Cooper said in a video.
“I didn’t see the IRGC out there, at all,” he added.
He said US forces were ensuring the strait’s shipping lanes remained free from Iranian sea mines after a major operation to remove the devices.
The US military says it has helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
Despite the progress, Iran continues to attack ships making the journey.
Oman said on Friday it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship that was targeted and set ablaze in the waterway. Iran reported three oil tankers were halted while transiting.
Meanwhile, a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials.
The visit took place a day after Iran said it had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance addressed to security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
The Wall Street Journal said the letter focused on a possible framework for negotiations.
Earlier in the week, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkike – members of the Makkah defense alliance – flew to Tehran for talks.

‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said. Photograph: ITV via Getty Images
‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said. Photograph: ITV via Getty Images
Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes
Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.
The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.
“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.
“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”
Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.
He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.
Keir Starmer alongside the US president, Donald Trump, at the Nato leaders’ summit in Ankara, Turkey in July. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.
“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.
“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”
His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.
As Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control?
Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.
Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.
Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.
“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.
“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

items.title: France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
items.summary: French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween, as some 320,000 people nationwide took to the streets.
items.content:
Europe roiled by more youth-led protests French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween, as some 320,000 people nationwide took to the streets.
France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
A demonstrator holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday.
PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.
Is this how the great international borrowing spree ends?
France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.
At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.
The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.
Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."
The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.
What Do The Protests Across Europe Mean For The Continent?
Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.
Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.
The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.
While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.
Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.
Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands
In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.
Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.
Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.
In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

The US oil industry has earned almost $130 billion in profits since the US and Israel began bombing Iran in February. The same companies, according to the New York Times , earned less than $47 billion over the same span of 2025, when oil was comparatively cheap.
Shipping and insurance costs have spiked thanks to the war, allowing oil companies to spike their prices. ExxonMobil and Chevron, the nation’s two largest fossil fuel corporations, saw profits surge. According to quarterly earnings reports released on Friday, ExxonMobil’s profits doubled over the same period last year, while Chevron’s grew by 180 percent. BP, another large oil company, reported its profits reached an 18-year high.
Shareholders are making money. President Donald Trump’s personal wealth in oil and gas stocks grew as much as $35.8 million this year, according to a report this week from congressional Democrats.
Americans, meanwhile, are paying the price—the median US household has spent $856 more at the gas pump than they otherwise would have since the war started.
The national average price of gasoline during the third quarter of 2026 was $4.12 a gallon, according to AAA—up 96 cents from a year ago and the highest ever quarterly price.
On the campaign trail, Trump has repeatedly attempted to assure Americans that this is a good thing: "The United States is the largest Oil Producer in the World, by far, so when oil prices go up, we make a lot of money," Trump wrote on Truth Social in March, just one month into the war. Seven months later, his pitch hasn’t changed.
“Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas, and they’re coming to Oklahoma, and they’re coming to Louisiana and they’re taking that oil,” he said at an October 24 campaign event in Georgia.
"I don't give a damn, I'm going to say it—we're making a freaking fortune."

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said all four vessels were carrying oil and that the ships had been halted following “incidents” or after hitting mines.
“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement on Friday.
Hours later, the IRGC said two more tankers – each carrying more than two million barrels of oil – “exploded and caught fire” as a result of hitting mines while attempting to pass through an “unauthorised route”.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Navy said on Friday that it struck and destroyed an unmanned enemy craft to the east of the strait.
Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran’s permission.
It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to transit Hormuz without authorisation would face “destruction”.
Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28.
The US military denies the naval mine claims. On Friday, United States Central Command chief Brad Cooper said the Strait of Hormuz’s “internationally recognised primary transit routes” had been successfully cleared of Iranian sea mines.
Shipping in the Strait of Hormuz is operating at about 70 percent below pre-war levels, the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday.

items.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
items.summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
items.content:
Image source, Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images
By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â  Reporting from New York
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (Â£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

items.content:
A worker shutters the windows of the luxury jewellery brand Tiffany & Co in Berlin on Friday, the day before the protests. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images
A worker shutters the windows of the luxury jewellery brand Tiffany & Co in Berlin on Friday, the day before the protests. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images
Cost of living protests to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween
Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing
Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.
Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.
In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service .
Students and activists block access to the Andreas-Gymnasium in Berlin this month in protest against compulsory military service and education cuts. Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/Shutterstock Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.
“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.
A Gen Z regelt poster in Leipzig announcing a protest on Saturday at Augustusplatz. Photograph: Maria Castro/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.
Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.
The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”
By Friday, more than 160,000 people had registered on the website saying they planned to attend the protests.
Students block the entrance to the Otto Suhr Institute of the Free University of Berlin this week under a banner saying: ‘Stop war research!’. Photograph: Volodymyr Sindieiev/Anadolu/Getty Images The federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.
It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on the marked decline in German school performance .
In France, the interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.
Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.
“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities ‌across France,” he said.
The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.
Protesters holding a French flag amid clashes during demonstrations in Paris last Saturday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.
In Paris, two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. An appeal by organisers against the decision to exclude them from the centre was rejected late on Friday night.
The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October .
Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.
Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

items.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
items.summary: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.
items.content:
By Jaroslav Lukiv Â  and Â  Joe Tidy ,Â  Cyber correspondent, BBC World Service
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist .
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle â cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

items.title: Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot
items.summary: Despite genocide, regional war and isolation, Israel's election revealed little appetite for political alternatives.
items.content:
Share Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot on social media
Palestinian boys stand amid the rubble after a building was hit overnight by an Israeli strike west of Jabalia in the northern Gaza Strip, [AFP]
After one of the highest voter turnouts in decades, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority in the October 27 polls.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Israel election result shows no overall majority as vote count complete
list 2 of 4 ‘Arab voice doesn’t count’: Jewish Israeli blocs reject Palestinian support
list 3 of 4 Coalition wrangling, a second election: How Israel could break the deadlock
list 4 of 4 Why is Netanyahu accusing Palestinian Israeli parties of fraud?
Netanyahu’s camp came first, with 53 seats, five more than the main opposition bloc. The Arab parties surged to a record 19 seats but have been relegated to merely observing coalition negotiations.
Viewed from a distance, the results could appear startling.
The judicial reforms ushered in at the start of Netanyahu’s government term in 2022 provoked the largest street protests in Israel’s history, while the prime minister himself is still embroiled in a  corruption trial dating back to 2019. Alleged failures ahead of the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip have still to be reckoned with, despite overwhelming public pressure to do so. Moreover, the genocide has led to growing international isolation, while also providing the pretext for multiple attacks on countries across the region – the latest of which, undertaken with the United States on Iran in February, continues to roil energy markets around the world.
Nevertheless, roughly 2.38 million Israelis on Tuesday made the journey to the polls to back Netanyahu’s coalition, led by his Likud party, while some 2.21 million cast their ballots for the opposition alliance.
Between the two, little space was given to examine the multiple war crimes Israel stands accused of having carried out in Gaza, where Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,500 people and left much of it in ruins, or government complicity in the surging violence and pogroms in the occupied West Bank, where a United Nations commission of inquiry said on Monday that Israel had been committing crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture and rape.
Analysts said the fact that neither Gaza nor the West Bank were a deciding factor in how Israelis voted on Tuesday was largely because they already represented an area of broad agreement across both alliances.
Instead, the election was fought on largely internal issues: the power of Israel’s courts, whether members of the ultra-Orthodox minority should be exempted from military service, and whether the government’s alleged culpability in missing the warnings of the October 2023 attack should be examined.
Leading Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani said the issues were pitched to the Israeli public along broadly similar lines to those used by the politicians enacting the policies.
“I don’t think the problem is simply that people are uninformed or disengaged,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Many Israelis know that Gaza has been devastated, even though they are exposed to a very selective representation of that devastation. But knowing something and recognising its moral and political implications are different things,” Shenhav-Shahrabani added, providing one explanation for the absence of empathy displayed by many Israelis in the face of the widely reported suffering of Palestinians in Gaza.
“Ordinary people, who love their families, care for their friends, and consider themselves decent human beings, can participate in or acquiesce to a political order that produces immense suffering for others,” he said.
For Shenhav-Shahrabani, there has been “a powerful mechanism of denial” at work. “Not necessarily denial of the facts, but denial of their meaning,” he said.
A Palestinian man walks through damaged makeshift shelters after an Israeli strike hit a nearby building the previous night, west of Jabalia in the northern Gaza Strip, on October 30, 2026 [AFP] Security on the agenda
For Netanyahu’s supporters, however, this denial could be traced to something more personal.
“The Likud is a tribe, or perhaps a cult and, as far as they are concerned, Dear Leader is always right,” Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman said of the prime minister’s base, which has sustained his rule for a cumulative 19 years – roughly a quarter of Israel’s entire existence.
“For them, the enemy, straight after the Arabs, is the left, and they would vote for Netanyahu regardless of his faults,” added Bregman, a senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.
For much of this electorate, the vote was less a judgement on the government’s conduct than a choice between competing claims to political legitimacy – or as Israeli academic Roi Zur put it, a contest over “the heart and soul of democracy” and the future of Jewish and Israeli identity.
“The most important thing, I think, for turnout among Netanyahu’s supporters is the understanding, or the belief, that the alternative coalition would be weaker on security,” said Zur, an expert on voter behaviour who teaches at Essex University.
What Netanyahu had been particularly successful in doing, he continued, was creating “this campaign of fear and the belief that he is the only one who can deal with this situation, that he is the only strong enough prime minister”.
“The idea that Netanyahu is the only and the strongest leader that can lead Israel through these recent times and the post-October 7 war.”
War and occupation, according to Shenhav-Shahrabani, were not choices to be made on the ballot paper.
Instead, they had become the prism through which, over decades, Israelis had come to view “security, citizenship, and the very meaning of democracy”.
“That is why replacing Netanyahu, important as it may be, would not by itself resolve the deeper problem.”

items.summary: As Russia’s war in Ukraine reshapes this Arctic frontier, Sámi communities struggle to sustain cross-border traditions.
items.content:
On the Norway-Russia border, the Sámi people face a growing divide
As Russia’s war in Ukraine reshapes this Arctic frontier, Sámi communities struggle to sustain cross-border traditions.
An illustration showing a map of the Indigenous coastal Sámi homeland, Sápmi, which stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s heavily militarized Kola Peninsula [Jawahir Al-Naimi/Al Jazeera]
An illustration showing a map of the Indigenous coastal Sámi homeland, Sápmi, which stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s heavily militarized Kola Peninsula [Jawahir Al-Naimi/Al Jazeera]
Share On the Norway-Russia border, the Sámi people face a growing divide on social media
Along the shores of the Neiden Fjord, in Norway’s northernmost county Finnmark, Nils Boine* gazes out across the water. On the horizon, the Neiden River splits around the craggy island of Skogerøya, but lurking beneath its surface is a fisherman’s bounty: hundreds of king crabs.
His grandmother was Sea Sámi, from an Indigenous coastal people whose homeland, Sápmi, stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s heavily militarised Kola Peninsula. In Finnmark’s fjords, Sea Sámi families have fished for generations. But these waters are dissected by more than currents and shoals. Since Norway and Russia fixed their border in 1826, Sámi communities in the region have been divided by a national boundary.
Two hundred years later, this Arctic community is a combination of Sámi, Norwegians, Finns, Ukrainians, Russians, and international seasonal workers. Most of the Sámi population lives in Norway, with roughly 2 percent residing in Russia.
The Sámi have established a cross-border lifestyle, supported by flexible policies, including a Norwegian-Russian agreement allowing visa-free travel for those living within 30km (18.5 miles) of the border.
Security, however, has begun to tighten since the onset of Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine. The West sees Finnmark as part of NATO’s exposed northern flank, as it is directly opposite Russia’s heavily armed Kola Peninsula. The Norwegian border town of Kirkenes has been caught in a spy war with Russia, with multiple Russian operatives having been caught posing as tourists and fishermen while trying to engage in espionage.
Now, border bureaucracy is a daily reality, and reindeer herding, language revitalisation and hunting traditions are increasingly being navigated through permits and regulations, making the wider Arctic infrastructure feel fractured.
“I have friends in Russia,” Boine says. “We used to go shopping in Russia, and go there for weekends.”
Since Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, those crossings have stopped — partly as a display of solidarity with Ukraine, and partly due to safety concerns.
“A local person was just arrested in Russia, so people are afraid to cross the border,” Boine explains. “The rumours say that he had some illegal things in his car, but he was arrested, and the [Ministry of] Foreign Affairs in Norway tried to do something, but it’s very difficult, of course, because we don’t have any diplomats in Russia.”
He is referring to the reported June arrest of a Kirkenes businessman. Lawyer John Christian Elden told the daily newspaper Verdens Gang (VG) that the man was in custody for two months under alleged “possession of weapons or ammunition". Some Kirkenes residents were left shaken by the news, as recreational hunting is common in the region. They fear accidentally crossing the Russian border with forgotten hunting ammunition that might be left in their cars.
The number of Russian tourists visiting Norway has also declined , from 250,000 in 2019 to 52,000 last year.
“Before, we had Russian guests, but not now,” Boine says. Fortunately for his family, who run a tourism company, 80 percent of customers come from Asia or Finland. Their business has emerged relatively unscathed, but other companies have not been as lucky.
“Shops in the area have lost a lot of income without Russian [tourists],” says Boine. “Several shops have had to close.”
In a landscape traditionally connected for centuries, the fragmentation of communities is deeply concerning for both the regional economy and Sámi culture. Cross-border connections are deeply rooted in the regional psyche.
For Boine, the war in Ukraine has put his friendships with people in Russia on hold.
“They are afraid to do something wrong or write something wrong,” he says quietly. “You never know what might happen if they have too close contact,” he says.
When tour guide Henrik Hoffmann hikes near the Norwegian-Russian border, he rarely sees other civilians [Courtesy of Kirkenes Tours]
When tour guide Henrik Hoffmann hikes near the Norwegian-Russian border, he rarely sees other civilians [Courtesy of Kirkenes Tours]
German Henrik Hoffmann visited Kirkenes in 2021 and fell in love with its landscape and tight-knit community. Deciding to relocate permanently, the expat co-founded a tourism company, Kirkenes Tours, and began working with Sámi herders and on hiking trails along the Norwegian-Russian border.
“I was nervous the first time,” Hoffmann admits. “I kept checking my maps to make sure I hadn’t accidentally crossed [the border].”
Distracted hikers can easily step over the border by mistake, as the frontier is only marked by posts and forest clearings.
Hoffmann takes tourists along these trails, teaching them about the border’s history and its strict rules, including heavy fines for touching a Russian marker. In June 2026, three Swedish tourists were reportedly each fined 8,000 Norwegian kroner ($830) for throwing stones across the border.
The terrain looks desolate, peppered with granite rocks and scattered birch trees, but it is well-surveilled. Watchtowers dot the horizon, and security cameras are tucked among branches overhead.
Hoffmann rarely sees other civilians on this route, but he has seen increasing numbers of Norwegian military patrols. When his walks are interrupted, it is mostly by Sámi-owned reindeer.
He points towards a small herd grazing in a sheltered valley beneath a rocky crag. The reindeer – which are marked with traditional branding and earmarks – are at least a kilometre (0.6 miles) away.
Sámi families use distinctive marks, including pre-approved patterns cut into reindeer ears, to instantly identify which animal belongs to which herder. In May and June, there is a calf marking round-up, where the local siida – an organisation of Sámi herders who manage reindeer – use huskies, snowmobiles and drones to track and herd reindeer into pens. This process ensures that every calf is correctly identified. The jagged earmarking is an ancient Indigenous practice.
Alongside traditional earmarking, Sámi herders have simplified these roundups with 21st-century technology. For years, they have attached GPS tracking devices to reindeer, enabling herders to locate livestock with ease. But this is no longer a reliable method, because the area along the Russian-Norwegian border is often affected by GPS jamming and spoofing.
Aeroplanes landing in Kirkenes have even been affected by the interference, with navigation symbols blocked or replaced with false location data. The same disruption can render reindeer trackers inaccurate and useless.
Recently, Russian interference has reportedly been targeting lower elevations, too, leaving those in the hills surrounding Kirkenes – typically hikers and reindeer herders – at higher risk of having a GPS device jammed or spoofed.
“I have experienced it saying I am in Tromsø,” says Hoffmann, referring to the northern Norwegian city, about an 800km (500 miles) drive from Kirkenes.
To avoid mishaps, he always hikes with a satellite phone, and many local reindeer herders now avoid using GPS trackers because they have become unreliable.
“Now, they’re mostly using GSM trackers, which rely on the phone network,” Hoffmann explains.
Reindeers graze along the Norwegian-Russian border and are rounded up at certain times of the year by Sámi herders [Eibhlis Gale-Coleman/Al Jazeera]
Reindeers graze along the Norwegian-Russian border and are rounded up at certain times of the year by Sámi herders [Eibhlis Gale-Coleman/Al Jazeera]
Walking through Finnmark's exposed borderlands means crossing paths with many types of wildlife, including the Arctic grouse, a bright-white bird that buries itself in the snow. But not all animal encounters are pleasant.
For Sámi herders, predators are an increasing concern. Finnmark’s brown bear population is steadily increasing, with bears freely crossing between Russian and Norwegian territory. Some residents believe the rise could be connected to a decline in Russian hunting activity, but since cross-border conservation has declined, it is difficult to say.
“Last year, a man was bitten,” says Hoffmann. He also reveals that at a local stable where his girlfriend goes horseback riding, a bear attacked a horse in its paddock.
Bear and wolf attacks are dangerous for reindeer, who spend much of the year wandering unattended in the remote Arctic terrain. Large animals, like bears, are also notorious for damaging reindeer fences, barriers key to preventing livestock from wandering into Russia.
For herders, these potential animal breaches illustrate how difficult it can be to control a border shaped as much by wilderness and animal wandering as by geopolitics. Norwegian authorities are now investing heavily in doing just that.
Following a report by the Norwegian National Police Directorate in 2024, the European Union awarded Norway 16.4 million euros ($18.5m) to strengthen its border surveillance. By 2033, Norway will have a fully operational Finnmark Brigade, forming a defensive presence throughout its Arctic region.
From the Arctic tundra along the Norwegian-Russian border, the Pasvik River is visible on the horizon [Eibhlis Gale-Coleman/Al Jazeera] Roaming wildlife is not following the same script. Along the Pasvik River, the boundary is visible, but it rarely feels fixed.
From the birch-covered slopes of the Norwegian side, the river forms a natural border, and coloured markers are dotted evenly along the water to help boaters navigate safely.
But by early November, the river is frozen, forming an icy bridge for the wandering wildlife – and a seasonal concern for Sámi herders who fear their reindeer will run off into Russia.
Across Sápmi, the terrain is already intersected by sections of reindeer fencing. Traditionally crafted from wood, these barricades discourage livestock from venturing into forbidden grazing lands, but these man-made structures have one weakness: On snowy winter days, large snowdrifts are enough to allow opportunistic reindeer to scramble across.
Along the border, efforts have intensified to try to prevent livestock from wandering into Russia, with increased patrols and repairs by herders.
In 2023, after 42 reindeer crossed into Russia in eight months, Norway moved to replace a dilapidated 7km (4.3-miles) of the 150km (93-mile) reindeer fence along the border. Still, some Sámi herders remain sceptical.
Egil Kalliainen, a local herder, told The Barents Observer that “reindeer will keep crossing the border with or without any war".
The trouble, many say, is that cross-border cooperation is needed. “Reindeer don’t understand borders,” Hoffmann says with a wry smile.
On the shelves of the Ä´vv Skolt Sámi Museum sit reindeer antlers that have been polished into pocketknife handles. Nearby, there are kuska cups carved from birch burl. These are examples of duodji, traditional Sámi handicraft created through techniques with cultural meanings that have been handed down for generations.
But duodji is more than an exhibit or souvenir; it is part of a broader economy rooted in reindeer herding, local materials and border exchange. Before the geopolitical tensions of recent years, Sámi artisans and institutions could easily move goods and sell jewellery made in Russia while maintaining connections across the region.
Barriers that hinder cultural exchange and trade directly impact the material foundation of Sámi culture.
by  Håkon Mudenia, political adviser to the Sámi Parliamentary Council
“Historically, national borders have divided Sámi and settlement areas,” said Håkon Mudenia, political adviser to the Sámi Parliamentary Council.
But now, border restrictions have made those exchanges more difficult, affecting the movement, sale and display of Sámi-made goods and limiting broader cultural cooperation. Mudenia says the council is calling for simplified customs and VAT rules for traditional Sámi handicrafts. “Barriers that hinder cultural exchange and trade directly impact the material foundation of Sámi culture,” he says.
Norwegian officials acknowledge the wider constraint. As a generational use of natural resources, duodji relies on raw materials, such as reindeer antlers or birch trees. These crafts play an important role in Sámi heritage preservation.
“Sanctions imposed on Russia have created constraints that affect the ability of Indigenous peoples to sustain cross‑border cooperation,” Marius Meisfjord Jøsevold, Norway’s state secretary at the Ministry of Local Government and Regional Development, tells Al Jazeera.
Duodji objects make Sámi culture visible, whether it is antler handles or leader pouches marked with a herder’s reindeer sign. But one part of the culture most threatened by a divided Sápmi boundary cannot be displayed on a museum shelf. It is spoken.
A Sami handler in traditional clothing holds two of his herd of reindeer in Saariselka, Finnish Lapland, in March 2013 [David McDougall/AP]
A Sami handler in traditional clothing holds two of his herd of reindeer in Saariselka, Finnish Lapland, in March 2013 [David McDougall/AP]
Centuries of colonisation have affected Indigenous languages in the region. Sápmi encompasses numerous Sámi communities and linguistic traditions, including Inari, Skolt and Sea Sámi communities. Each has distinct cultural differences, and there are nine surviving languages in total. Originally, the number was higher, but a handful of languages, including Akkala Sámi, are already extinct.
The 1826 delimitation of the Norwegian-Russian border was particularly damaging for Skolt Sámi lands. Separated across countries, the Skolt community faced an abrupt split.
From 1850 to 1959, the situation worsened , with Norwegianisation policies forcing Sámi children to be taught in Norwegian at state schools. As of 2026, local reports suggest there are fewer than 1,000 Skolt Sámi speakers across Norway, Finland and Russia.
“Border closures and restrictions render cross-border, all-Sámi cooperation more vulnerable,” explains Mudenia, noting that opportunities for speakers to gather are of utmost importance.
In 2026, the Sámi Parliament Council supported a Skolt Sámi Year of Culture, celebrating its distinct culture within the wider Indigenous community. But Mudenia says more must be done to protect and revitalise the community.
“The Sámi Parliament has already recognised Skolt Sámi as an official language in Norway and demands that the Norwegian Parliament do the same,” he says.
For the people living along this frontier, survival has long depended on forms of mutual care ...
The battle to protect the language is part of the ongoing demand for change. The Sámi Parliament Council wants a situation where Sámi economic, social and cultural conditions are safeguarded within national contingency plans, Mudenia explains.
“The overarching goal of the Sámi Parliament Council is to continuously dismantle border obstacles across Sápmi,” he says. “State security measures and geopolitical barriers must not be designed or implemented in a way that violates Indigenous rights, international law, or the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP).”
The council, he says, “thinks that Sámi communities should be included as an integral part of the total defence framework”, while Sámi expertise and representation should be “secured in national security and emergency preparedness forums to address such hybrid threats".
Jøsevold, from the Ministry of Local Government and Regional Development, says the Sámi Parliament is an important dialogue partner for the central government.
Asked about the council’s concerns, Jøsevold emphasised the government’s commitment to consultation as defence activity expands in the North. But he did not address Mudenia’s call for national recognition of the Skolt Sámi, or for Sámi representation in national-security forums.
“In Northern Norway, increased defence activity as a result of increased tensions caused by Russia’s illegal war against Ukraine will be coordinated with Sámi representatives to ensure due consideration to Sámi culture and traditional Sámi industries,” he says.
But for the people living along this frontier, survival has long depended on forms of mutual care that are not included in defence planning or government consultations.
Border markers along the Norwegian-Russian border: yellow is Norway, and red with green stripes is Russia [Eibhlis Gale-Coleman/Al Jazeera]
Border markers along the Norwegian-Russian border: yellow is Norway, and red with green stripes is Russia [Eibhlis Gale-Coleman/Al Jazeera]
“People think there is nothing here,” Hoffmann laughs as he scrambles up a steep embankment. The Pasvik River disappears behind the tree line, and an undulating expanse of smooth rock unfolds. A dark wooden cube appears on the horizon.
Set against a backdrop of the granite-speckled hillside, this building is a recreational shelter, one of the small public spaces designed to make the remote border landscape accessible year-round. It offers walkers, hikers, families, and herders alike a place to warm up and take shelter from the weather.
Inside, a fire sits ready to be lit; in winter, locals add an extra log before leaving, preheating the shelter for the next visitor. In another corner, a stack of children’s books forms the start of a community library.
Within these walls, it is easy to forget that NATO’s northernmost land border is a short walk away. One side of the shelter is a floor-to-ceiling window. The views are beautiful: rock-peppered hills and crevices, dipping and diving towards a hazy horizon. From this warm bench, nature is the star attraction, and the painted border markers stand forgotten.
Throughout the Varanger Peninsula, there is a determination to preserve everyday life. With the border just a few kilometres away, its largest city, Kirkenes, has become a multicultural Arctic outpost.
Along the harbour, tourists continue to disembark from Hurtigruten cruises, promising local business with their clockwork itineraries of border hikes and boat tours.
Reindeer roundups follow a seasonal calendar, not political agendas. Ocean vessels continue to collect nets of Arctic cod and baskets of king crabs, while along the Neiden River, Sámi fishermen return for the salmon season. In Kirkenes, a simple walk to the Joker supermarket could be interrupted by drifting conversations in Sámi, Norwegian, Finnish, Swedish, German, English or Russian.
“We were very surprised that we have people from Ukraine living in Kirkenes alongside Russian people in Kirkenes,” Boine admits. “I thought maybe there would be more conflict between these people, but not here.”
While many residents might have been surprised by Ukrainian refugees deciding to settle so close to the Russian border, Boine says it makes sense. “Because they speak Russian, it is easier for them to find work here,” he adds.
In February 2026, Barents Spektakel, an annual arts festival, marked the 200th anniversary of the Russian-Norwegian border. Kirkenes erupted in creative artwork and cultural displays, but the theme, “The border crossed us”, spoke volumes.
For Sámi communities, connection to these landscapes predates both the ongoing war and the 200-year-old border. There was an Arctic community before both, and across Sápmi, there is a growing determination that tightening borders will not erase it.
*Nils Boine is a pseudonym to protect the identity of a man with Sea Sámi heritage who lives near Neiden and crosses the border regularly.

US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

A worker rides a bicycle in front of the reactor building of the Bushehr nuclear power plant, just outside the southern city of Bushehr, in Iran [File: Majid Asgaripour/Mehr news agency/Handout via AP]
Several Iranian lawmakers have called for the country’s withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), as United States President Donald Trump says the war on Iran will be “wrapped up” soon.
The lawmakers’ demands come as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran this week to mediate peace talks with the US.
